Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Analyze the classification system of hallux rigidus and determine how it can aid in guiding
management.
Identify nonsurgical treatment options for the management of hallux rigidus.
Compare and contrast surgical treatment options for the management of hallux rigidus,
including open versus minimally invasive procedures, cheilectomy, arthroplasty, and fusion.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Definition and demographics

Spectrum of arthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint
Characterized by clinical signs/symptoms and radiographic findings
Leads to great toe pain, decreased MTP joint motion and function, and altered gait

Overview
Several signs and symptoms are associated with hallux rigidus. Patients experience
progressive loss of MTP joint motion, typically with greater loss of dorsiflexion than
plantar flexion. Patients have pain with push-off of the great toe during ambulation and
altered gait with lateral loading of the foot. Dorsal great toe prominence
(osteophyte/bump) often is present. Oblique shoe crease may be observed because of
lack of great toe dorsiflexion and a shift of weight laterally. Patients also report
interphalangeal joint pain of the great toe because the motion requirement for
dorsiflexion is moved from the MTP joint to the interphalangeal joint.
Radiographic findings include MTP joint space narrowing, dorsal lateral osteophyte
formation on the metatarsal head and the base of the proximal phalanx, cyst formation,
soft-tissue swelling, loose bone fragments at the dorsal MTP joint, and periarticular
sclerosis (Figure 1).

Figure 1 Weight-bearing lateral (A) and AP (B) radiographs of a foot demonstrate grade
III hallux rigidus. (Reproduced from Telleria JJM, Kwon JY: Hallux rigidus, in: Chou LB, ed:

Epidemiology
Affects 1 in 45 individuals older than 50 years1
Most common location of arthritis in the foot and ankle2
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
First metatarsal
Proximal phalanx
Sesamoids

Osteology
The first metatarsal articulates with the base of the proximal phalanx. Under the
metatarsal head and articulating with the metatarsal in grooves separated by the cristae,
the sesamoid sling, consisting of the medial and lateral sesamoids, moves as a unit,
coming into compressive contact in dorsiflexion of the great toe. The first MTP joint is
characterized as a condyloid joint.
Vascular Anatomy
Tibial artery
Dorsalis pedis artery
The tibial artery and dorsalis pedis artery provide blood supply for the first MTP joint.
Nerves
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
3/28

Dorsomedial cutaneous plantar nerve
Plantarmedial hallucal nerve
The dorsomedial cutaneous plantar nerve and the plantarmedial hallucal nerve supply the
hallux and the MTP articulation.
Tendons
Flexor hallucis longus
Flexor hallucis brevis
Extensor hallucis longus
Extensor hallucis brevis
Abductor hallucis
Adductor hallucis
Joints and Ligaments
Medial and lateral collateral ligaments
MTP joint and medial and lateral sesamoid articulations
Musculature
Flexor hallucis longus
Flexor hallucis brevis
Extensor hallucis longus
Extensor hallucis brevis
Abductor hallucis

Musculature
The flexor hallucis longus attaches to the plantar surface of the distal phalanx base, and
the flexor hallucis brevis attaches to the sesamoids and the plantar surface of the
proximal phalanx base, providing plantar flexion to the interphalangeal joint and the first
MTP joint, respectively. Similarly, on the dorsal aspect of the great toe, the extensor
hallucis longus and the extensor hallucis brevis provide dorsiflexion to the first MTP and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
4/28

interphalangeal joints. The abductor hallucis provides abduction to the first MTP joint,
and the adduction hallucis provides adduction to the first MTP joint.
Etiology
Repetitive trauma
Metabolic (gout) or inflammatory conditions
Genetics and foot structure
Metatarsus adductus
Hallux varus and hallux valgus
Flattened or chevron metatarsal head morphology
Sequela of trauma: dislocation, or malunion/nonunion of fracture of the MTP joint

Etiology
Many factors contribute to the pathology of hallux rigidus. Traumatic events, such as
jamming of the hallux or hyperextension injuries, commonly called turf toe injuries, may
lead to damage of the articular cartilage, which may lead to hallux rigidus.1 Systemic
inflammatory disorders may cause synovitis and eventual cartilage loss. Congenital
variations and foot structures that are thought to influence great toe motion, such as a
long first metatarsal bone, an irregular joint shape, a pronated foot, an abducted gait,
and flexor hallucis longus pathology may lead to hallux rigidus.1, 2 Hallux varus and
valgus may lead to joint incongruity and cartilage wear/loss.
Natural History
Eccentric joint loading
Excessive cartilage loading
Eccentric or excessive cartilage loading leads to cartilage loss and progressive arthritis.
Risk Factors
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
5/28

High-impact sports and injury

Risk Factors
Any injury to the first MTP joint may cause compressive injury or shear forces to the
joint.3 An example is a turf toe injury with hyperdorsiflexion of the great toe.
Classification
Hattrup and Johnson classification system
Coughlin classification system

Classification
The Hattrup and Johnson classification system is based on radiographic parameters.
Grade I is considered mild; the MTP joint space is maintained with the presence of a
dorsal osteophyte. Grade II is moderate disease and involves MTP joint space narrowing,
subchondral sclerosis, and moderate formation of osteophytes. Grade III is severe,
involving complete loss of joint space with marked formation of osteophytes.
The Coughlin classification system is based on radiographic parameters, clinical findings,
symptoms, and loss of MTP joint range of motion. Grade 0 is mild pain with activity and
minimal loss of motion. Dorsiflexion is 10% to 20% less than that of the contralateral
joint. Imaging studies appear normal. Grade 1 involves mild pain with activity, with
tenderness to palpation and a palpable dorsal spur. Dorsiflexion is 20% to 50% less than
that of the contralateral joint. Radiographic findings include a small dorsal spur but
minimal joint narrowing. A patient with grade 2 findings has pain related to activities of
daily living and difficulty with shoe wear because of palpable and tender osteophytes.
Dorsiflexion is 50% to 75% less than that of the contralateral joint. Typical radiographic
findings are mild to moderate joint space narrowing (<50%), sclerosis, and osteophyte
formation. Patients with grade 3 hallux rigidus have constant pain, tender and palpable
osteophytes, and dorsiflexion loss of 75% to 100% and plantar flexion loss of as much as
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
6/28

10%. They have pain with terminal range of motion. Radiographic findings include more
than 50% joint space narrowing and increased cystic and sclerotic changes. Grade 4 is
associated with physical examination and radiographic findings similar to those of grade
3 but with mid-arc range of motion. The Coughlin classification system has not been
found to be prognostic of outcomes. The clinical examination rather than the grading
system should guide management.4
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Pain
Swelling
Altered gait

Patient History
Patients have pain along the dorsal prominence over the MTP joint, shoe irritation, and
pain with push-off of the toe during ambulation because of impingement of the dorsal
osteophytes of the metatarsal head and the phalangeal base. Patients also may have
neuritic pain during closed shoe wear secondary to impingement of the dorsal sensory
nerve of the hallux. Swelling, warmth, and redness because of shoe irritation may be
present at the first MTP joint. Patients may have lateral foot pain because of lateral
loading of the foot and shifting foot plantar pressures from an altered gait.
Physical Examination
Tender dorsal prominence
Erythema
Decreased motion
Positive grind test
Plantar pain
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
7/28

Oblique shoe crease

Physical Examination
Patients commonly have a tender dorsal prominence and erythema from rubbing of the
shoe against the dorsal prominence. They may have dorsal impingement with
dorsiflexion and limited hallux range of motion. Patients also may have positive grind
test with axial loading of the first MTP joint. They also may have sesamoid tenderness
with plantar palpation, suggesting more advanced arthritis. An oblique shoe crease may
be observed because of the loss of first MTP motion and lateral loading.
Neurovascular Examination
Tinel sign
Toe numbness

Neurovascular Examination
Occasionally, patients may have a positive Tinel sign or toe numbness over the medial
eminence and the dorsal proximal and distal phalanx, elicited via compression or
traction of the dorsomedial hallucal nerve.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Weight-bearing AP, lateral, and oblique views
Occasionally, sesamoid views

Radiography
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
8/28

Specific signs to evaluate on radiographs include joint space narrowing, a dorsal
osteophyte at the base of the proximal phalanx and the metatarsal head, loose bodies in
the joint after a fracture of an osteophyte, cysts, and periarticular sclerosis. Sesamoid
radiographs may be obtained to evaluate for sesamoid arthritis if the patient has plantar
pain with palpation.
The horseshoe-shaped dorsal osteophytes of the first metatarsal head and the proximal
phalanx base may obscure the MTP joint space and overpredict joint space loss on AP
radiographs. Therefore, lateral radiographs, obtained appropriately perpendicular to the
joint, are the best view to determine the degree of joint space loss.
Pathology
Loss of articular cartilage of the MTP joint

Pathology
Loss of articular cartilage of the MTP joint varies. Cartilage loss most commonly affects
the dorsal aspect of the metatarsal head. With progression, cartilage wear may affect the
entire joint and the sesamoids. A central osteochondral defect of the cartilage is more
rare.
Diagnosis
Diagnosis is based on the clinical symptoms at the great toe MTP joint, physical examination
findings, and radiographic findings.
Differential Diagnosis
Crystalline disorders
Inflammatory arthritis
Septic arthritis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
9/28

Turf toe
Lumbar radiculopathy
Sesamoid pathology

Differential Diagnosis
The etiology of hallux rigidus may vary. Hallux rigidus may occur secondary to crystalline
disorders, such as gout and pseudogout; inflammatory or septic arthritis; turf toe or
other plantar plate injuries; lumbar radiculopathy with a footdrop or extensor hallucis
longus weakness, leading to altered great toe mechanics; or sesamoid pathology,
including sesamoiditis or sesamoid necrosis, resulting in cartilage damage.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Patient willingness to modify activities or pursue nonsurgical treatment
Patient with poor health

Indications
Nonsurgical treatment modalities typically are the mainstay of early management;
however, these treatment options depend on a patient’s willingness to comply with shoe
wear modifications and activity modifications. Nonsurgical treatment also is indicated in
patients with poor health limiting surgical treatment.
Contraindications
Medical comorbidities and drug interactions limit the use of NSAIDs.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
10/28


Contraindications
The use of NSAIDs is contraindicated in patients with a prior gastric ulcer, patients with
kidney disease, patients with high blood pressure, patients being treated with
anticoagulant agents, patients being treated with medications that may cause drug
interactions, and patients with other contraindications described on the medication
label.
Techniques/Procedures
NSAIDs
Corticosteroid injections
Activity modifications
Shoe wear modifications

Techniques/Procedures
Several nonsurgical treatment modalities can be attempted. Oral or topical NSAIDs can
be used. Corticosteroids can be injected into the first MTP joint; however, the literature
suggests that these injections are less effective than other foot injection sites (ie,
midfoot/hindfoot) and improvement for more than 3 months typically is only observed in
patients with mild disease.5 Activity modifications are important and include low-impact
activities and limiting inclines during hiking or if using a treadmill. A stiff full-length
orthosis, such as a carbon foot plate with or without a Morton extension, may help
protect the joint by limiting motion. Shoe modifications include stiffer soles, a rocker-
bottom, softer leather, and increased toe box depth to avoid impingement.
Surgical Management
Indications
Persistent pain
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
11/28

Surgical treatment is indicated in patients with continued great toe MTP joint symptoms
despite attempted nonsurgical treatment.
Contraindications
General comorbidities that preclude surgical management
General comorbidities that preclude surgical management include poor vascular supply; signs
of infection, including open ulceration or wounds; diabetes mellitus with a hemoglobin A1c
level greater than 8%; and inability to comply with postoperative restrictions.
Techniques/Procedures
Dorsal cheilectomy
Osteotomies
Interposition arthroplasty
Synthetic cartilage implants
Hemiarthroplasty
First MTP joint arthrodesis
Minimally invasive techniques

Techniques/Procedures
Joint-sparing options include open versus minimally invasive dorsal cheilectomy,
osteotomies, soft-tissue interposition arthroplasty, bony resection with interposition
arthroplasty, and synthetic cartilage implants. Advantages include decreased pain and
retained joint motion.
Dorsal cheilectomy is indicated in patients with mild to moderate hallux rigidus, isolated
dorsal great toe pain, and/or pain with push-off only. Contraindications include pain on
axial central grind testing or plantar great toe pain suggestive of sesamoid arthritis.
Dorsal cheilectomy can be performed in an open fashion or via minimally invasive
techniques. Dorsal cheilectomy involves resection of proximal phalanx and metatarsal
head osteophytes and the dorsal one-third of the articular surface of the metatarsal
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
12/28

head.6 Too much resection may lead to dorsal subluxation of the proximal phalanx.6 A
Moberg osteotomy (dorsiflexion osteotomy of the proximal phalanx) may be performed
if increased dorsiflexion positioning of the proximal phalanx is necessary or if hallux
interphalangeus is present (>10°) (Figure 2).
Figure 2 (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of a foot demonstrate joint space narrowing and
a dorsal osteophyte. The foot was managed via a dorsal cheilectomy. (Courtesy of Judith
F. Baumhauer, MD, MPH, FAAOS, Rochester, NY.)
Isolated soft-tissue interposition arthroplasty is indicated for the management of mild to
moderate hallux rigidus. Patients may have pain on grind testing, dorsal great toe pain,
and/or pain with push-off. This procedure is contraindicated in patients with plantar first
MTP joint pain suggestive of sesamoid arthritis because the sesamoids are not
resurfaced or covered. Resurfacing of the metatarsal head with tissue allows for a gliding
surface after removal of the dorsal osteophytes of the metatarsal head and the phalanx.
The metatarsal head is resurfaced via placement of autograft or allograft tissue using
hallucis brevis, dorsal capsule, or skin substitute.
More extensive bony resection of the proximal phalanx with interposition arthroplasty
may be considered in patients with mild to moderate hallux rigidus. Indications include
pain on grind testing and dorsal great toe pain and/or pain with push-off. This procedure
should not be performed in patients with plantar great toe pain suggestive of sesamoid
arthritis. Many techniques have been described, one of which is the modified oblique
Keller capsular interposition arthroplasty.7 This technique involves a dorsal cheilectomy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
13/28

of the first metatarsal followed by an oblique cut of the proximal phalanx. The
attachments of the plantar fascia and the plantar plate are preserved. The capsular soft
tissue and the extensor hallucis brevis are advanced into the MTP joint and used for
resurfacing.
The use of a synthetic cartilage implant (hydrogel) may be considered in patients with
moderate to severe hallux rigidus (Figure 3). Patients may have pain on grind testing,
dorsal great toe pain, and/or pain with push-off. This procedure should be avoided in
patients with plantar great toe pain suggestive of sesamoid arthritis. The polyvinyl
alcohol hydrogel interposition implant is placed into a drill hole made in the metatarsal
head. The implant is left 2 to 3 mm proud and functions as a joint spacer. A synthetic
cartilage implant is associated with advantages, such as preservation of joint motion;
however, careful patient selection and precise surgical technique are required to
optimize outcomes.8 If failure with recurrent pain in the first MTP joint occurs,
conversion to fusion can be performed, with results equivalent to those of primary great
toe fusion (Figure 4).
Figure 3 Intraoperative photograph of a foot shows correct positioning of the implant in
the first metatarsal. (Reproduced from Telleria JJM, Kwon JY: Hallux rigidus, in Chou LB,
ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Foot and Ankle, Ed 6. Rosemont, IL, American Academy
of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 191-204.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
14/28

Figure 4 Preoperative (A) and postoperative (B) AP foot radiographs demonstrate
management with the use of a synthetic cartilage implant. (Courtesy of Judith F.
Baumhauer, MD, MPH, FAAOS, Rochester, NY.)
Joint-sacrificing options include hemiarthroplasty and first MTP joint arthrodesis. Several
hemiarthroplasty implants have been described, including metallic, silicone, and plastic
implants. They may be placed in the proximal phalanx or the metatarsal head. Single and
comparative longitudinal studies with short-term follow-up data have suggested good
pain relief and functional improvement; however, midterm and long-term studies
(follow-up of 5 or more years) have reported implant loosening, transfer metatarsalgia,
and the need for revision surgery with interposition grafts to attempt to restore first ray
length and function. Overall, the results are poorer than those of primary great toe
fusion, and failure requires a more extensive revision plan with poorer outcomes than
those of primary great toe fusion (Figure 5).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
15/28

Figure 5 Radiographs of the left foot of a patient with ongoing pain. Preoperative AP (A)
and lateral (B) radiographs demonstrate failed hemiarthroplasty. Postoperative AP (C)
and lateral (D) radiographs demonstrate implant removal and arthrodesis of the first
metatarsophalangeal joint. (Courtesy of Judith F. Baumhauer, MD, MPH, FAAOS,
Rochester, NY.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
16/28

First MTP joint arthrodesis affords reliable pain relief in patients with moderate to severe
hallux rigidus. Arthrodesis is indicated in patients who have pain on grind testing, dorsal
great toe pain, and/or pain with push-off, with or without plantar great toe pain
suggestive of sesamoid arthritis. The toe is positioned in neutral rotation, with 5° to 15°
of dorsiflexion relative to the floor or approximately 25° relative to the declination angle
of the first metatarsal, and 10° to 15° of valgus or adjacent to the second toe.6 The
relationship to foot alignment (cavus or pes planus) and the adjacent toes must be
considered in determination of the fusion position. A flat plate may be used to simulate
weight bearing, which helps guide positioning. Simulated weight bearing should
demonstrate the toe pulp to be lightly resting on the plate and the interphalangeal joint
to be able to be extended to 5° of dorsiflexion. The combination of a compression lag
screw and a dorsal plate has been shown to be the most biomechanically stable
construct (Figure 6).
Figure 6 Images of the foot of a patient with hallux rigidus. Preoperative AP (A), lateral
(B), and lateral oblique (C) radiographs demonstrate advanced hallux rigidus.
Postoperative AP (D), lateral (E), and lateral oblique (F) radiographs demonstrate first
metatarsophalangeal joint fusion. (Courtesy of Judith F. Baumhauer, MD, MPH, FAAOS,
Rochester, NY.) 
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
17/28

Preoperative Planning
Evaluate preoperative imaging studies.
Ensure proper equipment is available.

Preoperative Planning
Assess the relative length and position of the first metatarsal compared with the second,
third, fourth, and fifth metatarsals. Excessive shortening may lead to lateral loading and
metatarsalgia. Evaluate for cystic changes in the first metatarsal head because bone
grafting may be necessary in patients with a large bony defect.
Implants, hardware, and procedure-specific instrumentation must be readily available.
The use of mini fluoroscopy is optimal.
Patient Positioning
Supine position
Supine positioning with a bump placed under the ipsilateral hip may aid in positioning the toe
in a perpendicular orientation.
Surgical Approaches
Dorsal or medial approach

Surgical Approaches
Dorsal or medial approaches to the hallux can be used. The dorsal approach is medial to
the extensor hallucis longus tendon and centered on the first MTP joint, whereas the
medial approach is centered longitudinally on the first MTP joint (Video 1).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
18/28

Video 1 Charlton T, Gonzalez T, Thordarson DB: Current Concepts in the Management of
Advanced/End-Stage Hallux Rigidus [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2019. https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-
page/20298__Videos. Accessed May 6, 2021.
Postoperative Management
Weight bearing and immobilization depend on the procedure performed.
Formal physical therapy is optional.

Postoperative Management
Postoperative management after open or minimally invasive dorsal cheilectomy and
synthetic cartilage implantation includes the use of a postoperative shoe for 2 to 3 weeks
until the wound heals, followed by the use of a regular shoe. After open or minimally
invasive fusion or modified oblique Keller capsular interposition arthroplasty, weight
bearing is limited for 1 to 2 weeks in a postoperative shoe, cast, or boot, after which
weight bearing is progressed as tolerated for an additional 4 weeks. Patients are
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
19/28

transitioned to a shoe as tolerated at 6 to 12 weeks postoperatively. If fusion is
performed, MTP dorsiflexion should be avoided until radiographic union is observed.
Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
Excessive resection of the base of the proximal phalanx during arthroplasty may result in loss
of the plantar plate and flexor hallucis brevis attachments. This allows the sesamoids to
migrate proximally. In addition, the MTP joint will dorsiflex, and a flexion contracture will
develop in the interphalangeal joint. Stress transfer to the second MTP joint may lead to
symptoms spreading across the forefoot.
P-contoured first MTP fusion plates should be used with caution because they may result in
poor toe positioning.
DVT prophylaxis
Patient comorbidities

Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
Pre-contoured plates may result in malpositioning of the toe because different foot
alignments have different dorsiflexion requirements of the first MTP joint.
DVT prophylaxis is used for all patients and ranges from aspirin to full anticoagulation,
depending on patient risk factors. Vitamin D levels may be low in some patient
populations, and vitamin D supplementation may be necessary. Patients being treated
with rheumatoid biologic medications may have delayed skin and bone healing, and the
time for weight bearing and casting/boot use may need to be adjusted because of these
issues. In patients with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, surgical treatment should be
postponed until control is improved, as assessed via hemoglobin A1c levels.
Complications
Nonunion
Nonunion of first MTP fusion occurs in zero to 8.9% of patients.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
20/28


Nonunion
First MTP open fusion results in high union rates (90% to 100%).3 Despite the overall
excellent functional outcomes, a risk for nonunion exists. Nonunion of first MTP fusion
occurs in zero to 8.9% of patients, depending on the technique used.3 Fewer than 40% of
nonunions are symptomatic.9 Minimally invasive first MTP fusion rates are comparable
with those of open first MTP fusion rates.10
Malunion/Malalignment
Rotational, varus-valgus, and dorsiflexion–plantar flexion malunion are possible secondary to
technical error.6
Malalignment of first MTP joint after arthrodesis may lead to difficulties in toe-off or
interphalangeal joint osteoarthrosis.

Malunion/Malalignments
Fitzgerald11 reported a 16% malalignment rate in their patient cohort.11 Malunion
secondary to technical error occurred in the transverse, sagittal, and frontal planes.11
Malunion, such as inadequate valgus or inadequate dorsiflexion, may lead to excessive
loads on the interphalangeal joint of the great toe and progressive arthritic changes,
causing pain.
Malalignment of the first MTP joint after arthrodesis may lead to difficulty in toe-off or
osteoarthrosis of the interphalangeal joint if placed in less than 5° to 10° of valgus.6
Excessive varus force on the interphalangeal joint after fusion may lead to
interphalangeal joint arthritis.6 The rate of symptomatic arthritis of the interphalangeal
joint after a first MTP joint malunion is less than 5%.6
Pain
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
21/28

Inadequate bone resection during cheilectomy may lead to continued pain.
Transfer metatarsalgia, clawing of the hallux, or cock-up deformity is possible with modified
oblique Keller capsular interpositional arthroplasty.
Metatarsalgia
Painful hardware
Persistent metatarsal sesamoid arthritis

Pain
Patients may have continued pain secondary to impingement after a dorsal cheilectomy
if bone resection is inadequate. Modified oblique Keller capsular interpositional
arthroplasty may lead to transfer metatarsalgia, clawing of the hallux, or cock-up
deformity;7,12 however, leaving the flexor hallucis brevis tendon intact is reported to be
the key to reducing overall complications.7,12 Metatarsalgia may develop or worsen after
first MTP fusion if malunion is present.6 Lateral foot overload may occur with plantar
flexion malunion after first MTP fusion.6 Painful hardware may necessitate hardware
removal.
Infection
Infection rate less than 2%
The risk of infection is similar to that of other elective surgical procedures.
Fracture
Fractures are possible.
Hardware Failure
Arthroplasty failure may result from component loosening, loss of bone stock, osteolysis,
implant subsidence, decreased range of motion, or continued pain.
Possible adverse events related to synthetic cartilage implants include malpositioning,
loosening, implant wear, erosion into the proximal phalanx, continued pain, and stiffness.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:19 PM
AAOS | Hallux Rigidus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002006
22/28

Nonunion of great toe fusion may lead to implant fatigue and fracture.

Hardware Failure
Results of arthroplasty may vary, depending on the type of implant used. Historically,
silastic-based components were used, which led to synovitis and osteolysis; these
implants have since been abandoned because of the rate of failure.6 Other designs have
used cobalt-chromium alloy or metal-on-polyethylene bearings, which have resulted in
hardware failure secondary to technical errors, implant subsidence, loss of bone stock,
osteolysis, decreased range of motion, and continued pain.
Possible adverse events related to synthetic cartilage implants include malpositioning,
loosening, implant wear, erosion into the proximal phalanx, continued pain, and
stiffness. Baumhauer et al4 reported that approximately 9% of patients required implant
removal because of persistent pain at a follow-up of 2 years and approximately 14%
required implant removal at a follow-up of 5.8 years.
Instability
Excessive resection during cheilectomy may lead to instability.

Instability
Excessive bone resection during dorsal cheilectomy may lead to dorsal translation of the
proximal phalanx on the metatarsal head and subsequent shear of the joint.13
Patients with risk factors or a history of venous thromboembolism may require full
prophylactic anticoagulation.

Dorsomedial cutaneous nerve of the hallux and plantarmedial hallucal nerve at risk

Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
The dorsomedial cutaneous nerve of the hallux is at risk with the surgical approach.
Injury to the nerve may result in numbness, paresthesia, and neuritic pain. The
plantarmedial hallucal nerve is at risk if sutures are placed in the plantarmedial capsule
via the interposition graft placement technique.
Other Complications
Additional procedures may be necessary if arthritis encountered intraoperatively is more
substantial than that observed before a cheilectomy or joint-sparing procedure.
Dorsal cheilectomy is associated with a risk of progressive arthritis and pain with isolated
resection or a lack of toe positioning despite resection, leading to the need for a dorsiflexion
osteotomy of the proximal phalanx (Moberg osteotomy) or eventual conversion to fusion.
Minimally invasive cheilectomy is associated with thermal injury, nerve damage, wound
complications, iatrogenic cartilage damage, and higher revision surgery rates.14
Outcomes
Satisfaction rates ranging from 88% to 95% have been reported after cheilectomy. Early
outcomes after minimally invasive cheilectomy are promising.14
Rates of fusion after arthrodesis range from 90% to 100%.3 Minimally invasive versus open
first MTP fusion result in similar fusion and complication rates. A slightly higher incidence of
hardware removal is associated with minimally invasive first MTP fusion; however, longer term
studies are necessary.10
Synthetic cartilage implantation is a reasonable alternative to fusion in carefully selected
patients.
Interpositional arthroplasty results in good to excellent outcomes with preserved motion.
Inconsistent data on the results of hemiarthroplasty
Results for modified oblique Keller interposition arthroplasty include good first MTP motion.

Outcomes
Level IV studies demonstrate satisfaction rates ranging from 88% to 95% after
cheilectomy in patients with dorsal pain; however, patients with pain in the middle range
of motion have lower satisfaction scores.12 Improvement in dorsiflexion of 21.7° to 40°
has been reported.12 Theoretic advantages of minimally invasive cheilectomy include
decreased wound complications, improved cosmesis, and less soft-tissue disruption,
which may lead to improved range of motion and function. Studies examining the early
and midterm outcomes of open versus minimally invasive cheilectomy report similar
improvements in pain, function, and range of motion; however, higher revision surgery
rates are associated with minimally invasive cheilectomy, indicating that longer term
data are necessary.14
In a Level I prospective, randomized study and subsequent follow-up series, patients
who underwent synthetic cartilage implantation reported excellent pain relief (90%) and
function, with maintained first MTP motion at a follow-up of 2 years and 5.8 years.4, 15
Synthetic cartilage implantation is a reasonable alternative to fusion because of shorter
surgical time and preservation of joint motion; however, concerns for implant
subsidence, variable patient satisfaction, and radiographic complications exist.8 Careful
patient selection and precise surgical technique are necssary to optimize outcomes.
Level IV studies on interpositional arthroplasty have demonstrated good to excellent
results in 94% of patients, with preserved motion without instability.3 Aynardi et al16
noted that 90% of their cohort had excellent or good patient-reported outcomes, with an
overall failure rate of 3.8%. However, Deland and Williams12 noted transfer
metatarsalgia in four of seven patients. Level IV studies on hemiarthroplasty have
demonstrated inconsistent data on short-term follow-up. The current recommendation
is that hemiarthroplasty should be limited to patients with low-demand activity levels.12
